How do I connect M5 Smart to the app?
Open the Momcozy App and make sure Bluetooth is enabled.
Tap Add Device, select M5 Smart, or scan the QR code on the pump.
Once connected, you’ll see the control page.
Can I control both pumps at the same time?
Yes. The app supports dual control , so you can adjust both pumps together with one tap.
You can also switch between left / right pump control and set different modes or suction levels for each side.
Can I connect M5 Smart to multiple phones?
For the best experience, connect to one phone at a time.
If you want to switch phones, disconnect from the current device first and pair again on the new phone.
Can I use M5 Smart without the app?
Yes. The Momcozy App is optional—M5 Smart can also be used directly with the pump controls.
What can I control in the app?
Once connected, you can start/stop pumping, switch modes, adjust suction levels, and check key pump status (such as battery level) right from the Momcozy App .
What kind of pumping stats can I view in the app?
The app can show a clear overview of your pumping records, including:
Daily / weekly / monthly summaries
Total logged output (based on manual entries)
Session frequency and duration
What's the difference between M5 Smart and M5?
M5 Smart is an upgraded version of M5 with app control and longer battery life.
You can adjust modes and suction levels right from your phone—no need to reach into your bra or fumble with buttons during a session. The app also helps you log milk output and pumping sessions, so you can stay organized and track your routine more easily.
M5 Smart also lasts longer (up to 180 mins vs. 150 mins), while keeping the same compact, fully in-bra design.
Why is pumping with M5 Smart more comfortable than other pumps?
M5 Smart is made to feel gentler and easier to wear. The DoubleFit™ flange and baby mouth-like suction rhythm help create a softer, more natural-feeling pumping experience. With 30-minute auto stop and an 8 oz ultra-light design, it’s more comfortable for everyday pumping—at home, at work, or on the go.

Is Momcozy M9 hospital-grade breast pump?
Momcozy M9 is a wearable, personal breast pump with hospital-grade suction power . It is helpful to know the distinction between a "hospital-grade" pump and "hospital-grade suction."
A "hospital-grade" breast pump is really a multi-user, rental pump designed for use in a hospital or clinic setting. They are made in a closed system so the milk won't get into the motor or tubing, so they can be shared with many mothers safely. They are most commonly for moms who need to establish their milk supply or moms with a baby in the NICU.
On the other hand, "hospital-grade suction power" refers to the suction power and cycle rate of the pump. This is used to refer to a pump that can produce sufficient suction to well initiate and maintain a milk supply by mimicking a powerful suckling baby.
Brief and to the point, the Momcozy M9 delivers powerful performance you need in a convenient, hands-free configuration that's perfect for personal, in-your-home-on-the-go applications. Unless you have a medical need for a multi-user pump, a personal pump with hospital-grade suction like the M9 should be ample power for your daily pumping needs.

Is It Good to Use Electric Breast Pumps?
Yes! Electric breast pumps are a great choice for breastfeeding moms looking for convenience and efficiency. They can help maintain or increase milk supply, especially for working mothers or those with low supply issues. Choosing the right electric breast pump means finding one that offers strong suction power, quiet operation, and easy-to-use features. A comfortable and effective electric breast pump can make your breastfeeding journey smoother and more successful.
How Many Minutes Should I Use an Electric Breast Pump?
For most moms, starting with 15–20 minutes per pumping session is recommended, gradually adjusting based on your milk supply and comfort. Every mom’s needs are different, so listen to your body and pump according to what feels best for you.
Factors like your milk production, your baby’s feeding schedule, and your comfort all play a role. Stop pumping if you feel any discomfort or when your breasts feel empty to avoid over-pumping, which can cause soreness or irritation. Using your electric breast pump correctly helps maintain a healthy milk supply and a comfortable breastfeeding experience.
Do Wearable Pumps Decrease Milk Supply?
A wearable pump does not decrease milk supply, as long as it provides strong and effective suction. Suction strength is key to fully emptying the breast, which helps maintain a healthy milk supply.
Wearable pumps like the Momcozy S12 Pro are designed with high suction power to ensure efficient milk removal, so you can pump hands-free without compromising your milk production.
Which Is Less Painful: Manual or Electric Breast Pump?
Pain during pumping varies from mom to mom, but many breastfeeding mothers find electric breast pumps to be less painful because they offer multiple adjustable suction levels and modes, allowing you to customize comfort and reduce nipple pain. However, using too high suction, especially with sensitive nipples or elastic nipples, can still cause discomfort.
Some moms prefer manual breast pumps because they provide more control over suction and pumping speed, which can help minimize pain. Yet, manual pumps may cause hand and wrist fatigue when used for long sessions.
Regardless of whether you choose a manual or electric breast pump, selecting the right breast pump flange size and adjusting the suction level correctly are essential for reducing pain, preventing nipple soreness, and ensuring a comfortable pumping experience.
How Do I Choose an Electric Breast Pump?
Choosing the right electric breast pump can make all the difference for busy moms. Here are key factors to consider:
Portability: If you pump on the go or at work, choose a lightweight, portable breast pump like the Momcozy M6 that fits your lifestyle.
Suction Power: Look for a pump with strong and adjustable suction to effectively express milk and maintain a healthy milk supply.
Comfort: The right fit matters — try different pumps and flanges to find one that feels comfortable and prevents nipple pain or discomfort.
Features: Consider useful features such as double pumping for efficiency, quiet operation for discretion, rechargeable batteries for convenience, and app control for personalized pumping sessions.
Picking the right electric breast pump tailored to your needs helps make breastfeeding easier, more comfortable, and more efficient.
How should I clean and sterilize M6 accessories?
Wash M6 accessories with regular dish soap. If sterilization is needed, boil them for 5 minutes, then air dry, wipe dry, or use low-temperature drying. Do not use microwave sterilization. For steam sterilizing, drying, or hot-air drying, keep the temperature within 100°C / 212°F when possible and do not exceed 110°C / 230°F. M6 accessories can also be cleaned in a Momcozy bottle washer, but please do not use Storage mode. Avoid alcohol-based cleaners, as they may affect the soft silicone on the flange.
Why does the suction feel weaker after cleaning or sterilizing?
Suction may feel weaker if the milk collector or flange is slightly deformed after excessive heat exposure, which can affect the airtight seal. Please check whether the accessories are fully dry, properly installed, and free from warping, gaps, or damage. To help maintain strong suction, avoid microwave sterilization and keep steam sterilizing, drying, or hot-air drying within the recommended temperature range.

Every Detail, Thoughtfully Designed
What is the Momcozy Wellness 1 warm-massage breast pump and why do the warmth and massage features help with milk flow?
The Momcozy Wellness 1 (Momcozy W1) is a warm-massage breast pump. It is the first wearable pump to use our industry-first rhythmic massage and wraparound warmth. This combined approach is key:
1. The gentle heat relaxes your breast tissue and milk ducts, just like a warm compress.
2. The rhythmic massage breast pump uses soothing vibrations to mimic a baby’s natural touch. This helps your body release oxytocin—the hormone needed for milk let-down—making the milk flow smoother and faster.
How does the heating feature on the Momcozy W1 work, and is it a safe heated breast pump?
The Momcozy W1 has an industry-first wraparound warmth design. This heat feature works like a built-in warm compress on the flange area. It gives wide, gentle, comforting warmth that helps your breast relax and respond naturally. The temperatures are very carefully controlled to be safe.
What is the difference between the Momcozy W1 and the Air 1?
The Momcozy Wellness 1 represents a significant shift from the Air 1. The major improvement in the W1 is the inclusion of the industry-first integrated heat and advanced rhythmic vibration massage pump technology, which the Air 1 lacks. In contrast to the Air 1, which features app connectivity and a charging case, the Momcozy W1 focuses purely on wearable comfort, warmth, and massage and app enabled but doesn't include charging case. The core benefit of the Momcozy W1 is the therapeutic warm-massage breast pump experience.
How does the Momcozy W1 compare to a standard pump?
The Momcozy W1 is both a powerful wearable pump and a heated breast pump. Standard pumps only use suction. The Momcozy W1 adds our rhythmic massage and wraparound warmth. People call it the ultimate warm-massage breast pump because the heat and massage relax your body for better milk expression.
Has the Momcozy Wellness 1 been tested for safety and does it have certifications?
Yes, absolutely! We tested the motor and all parts of the Momcozy Wellness 1 very carefully. Experts checked them to make sure they are safe, strong, and will last a long time. Rest assured that this warm-massage breast pump complies with all relevant safety standards and certifications, making it a reliable tool for your entire feeding journey.
Does the pump come with accessories or spare parts?
Yes, the Momcozy W1 includes all essential parts you need to start pumping right immediately. We also include different inserts for the flanges to meet various sizing needs, ensuring you get the perfect fit for your warm breast pump. We also offer other spare parts (like valves or collection cups) for separate purchase.
Does the Momcozy W1 require an app to work?
The Momcozy W1 offers total flexibility and can be used with or without an app . While the built-in LED display allows for easy manual adjustments, connecting to the app provides smart control right from your phone so you can adjust suction, warmth, and massage without needing to fumble under your blouse. Additionally, you can access expert modes ready in one tap that are specifically designed to support milk flow and make late-night pumping sessions much easier to handle.
Does W1 come with a charging case?
The W1 does not include a separate charging case, but its built-in battery power is so strong that it matches the performance of pumps with a case .
It features a high-capacity 2200 mAh battery , which is much larger than many other wearable pumps. This design allows the W1 to be powerful yet simple to carry.
On a single full charge, the W1 provides industry-leading runtime:
Up to 10 sessions (Standard Mode) — for reference, some pumps with charging cases offer around 15 sessions in total, making the W1’s 10-session standalone power very impressive.
Up to 6 sessions (Warm-Massage Mode)
This high-capacity design ensures you have enough power for both day and night use without needing to carry a bulky extra charging case.
Is there a carrying or travel bag included?
W1 does not include a dedicated carrying or travel bag by default.
Its compact design makes it easy to store in most personal bags, backpacks, or baby bags.

Czym jest Lejek DoubleFit™ i dlaczego jest wyjątkowy?
Ekskluzywny Lejek DoubleFit™ firmy Momcozy łączy w sobie:

● Sztywny PP: zapewnia stabilność i bezpieczne, szczelne zamknięcie.

Została zaprojektowana tak, aby naśladować naturalne uczucie dotyku dziecka, zapewniając jednocześnie stabilne ssanie, komfort i wydajność podczas odciągania pokarmu. Dzięki temu stanowi rozwiązanie jako najlepszy laktator dla osób poszukujących efektywnego i komfortowego sposobu odciągania mleka.
Jak działa rytmiczne pompowanie?
S12 Pro Quick oferuje 3 tryby × 9 poziomów intensywności, zaprojektowane tak, aby symulować naturalne ssanie dziecka:
● Tryb stymulacji: krótkie, delikatne impulsy, które pobudzają wypływ mleka.
● Tryb odciągania: głębokie, dłuższe cykle, które pozwalają skutecznie odciągać mleko.
● Tryb mieszany: naprzemienne krótkie impulsy stymulujące i głębsze odciąganie, które pozwalają całkowicie opróżnić pierś.
Pomaga to szybciej pobudzić wypływ mleka, zwiększyć jego ilość i wygodnie opróżnić pierś, co czyni urządzenie efektywnym jako laktator elektryczny.
Czy jest łatwy w montażu i czyszczeniu?
Oczywiście. Każdy element został zaprojektowany z myślą o łatwości użytkowania, co czyni ten laktator wyjątkowo prostym w obsłudze:
● Szybki montaż czterech części dzięki oznaczeniom u góry, które ułatwiają precyzyjne dopasowanie.
● Usprawniony zawór typu „duckbill”: większy, prosty w konstrukcji, łatwy w montażu i demontażu bez ryzyka utraty elementów.
● Jednoczęściowa konstrukcja lejka: eliminuje trudne do czyszczenia narożniki i gromadzenie się zanieczyszczeń.
● Łatwe czyszczenie: wystarczy opłukać, wysuszyć i gotowe.
Wszystko po to, aby skrócić czas potrzebny na montaż i czyszczenie, pozostawiając więcej czasu dla Ciebie i Twojego dziecka.

Czy jest wystarczająco cicho, aby dyskretnie pompować?
Tak. Bezszelestne działanie o poziomie hałasu ≤46 dB pozwala na dyskretne odciąganie pokarmu w domu, w biurze lub w innym miejscu bez przeszkadz, co czyni go rozwiązaniem jako najlepszy laktator.
Co jest wyjątkowego w konstrukcji uchwytu?
Innowacyjna konstrukcja uchwytu została zainspirowana rzeczywistymi sytuacjami podczas odciągania pokarmu i sprawia, że ten laktator muszlowy jest wygodny w codziennym użytkowaniu:
● Łatwy uchwyt: szybkie zakładanie i zdejmowanie pojemnika na mleko, nawet mokrymi rękami.
● Pokrywa lejeka 2 w 1: pełni funkcję osłony przeciwpyłowej i stabilnej podstawki, zapobiegającej rozlaniu pokarmu.
Odciągaj pokarm bez obaw i zminimalizuj bałagan lub przypadkowe przewrócenie.
Czy mogę dostosować siłę ssania i prędkość?
Tak. Intuicyjny cyfrowy panel sterowania i wyświetlacz LCD umożliwiają w tym laktator elektryczny:
● Uruchamianie, wstrzymywanie i regulację poziomu ssania
● Wybór preferowanego trybu pompowania
● Monitorowanie czasu trwania sesji i stanu baterii
Dostosuj każdą sesję do swoich potrzeb i zmaksymalizuj jej efektywność.
Czy pompa jest bezpieczna dla mojego dziecka?
Tak. Wszystkie elementy mające kontakt z mlekiem są wolne od BPA i wykonane z PP i silikonu dopuszczonych do kontaktu z żywnością. Każda część została zaprojektowana tak, aby spełniała surowe normy bezpieczeństwa dotyczące zdrowia dziecka, co czyni ten laktator bezpiecznym rozwiązaniem.
Czy mogę używać tej pompy w podróży?
Oczywiście. Dzięki niewielkiej wadze 240 g, kompaktowej konstrukcji, długiej żywotności baterii wystarczającej na 8 sesji oraz cichej pracy na poziomie ≤46 dB, S12 Pro Quick jako laktator bezprzewodowy jest idealnym rozwiązaniem dla mam, które potrzebują mobilności i elastyczności.

Google Ads is dedicated to following advertising regulations for healthcare and medicine, so ads and destinations are expected to follow appropriate laws and industry standards. Some types of healthcare-related content can’t be advertised at all, while others can only be advertised in certain locations by advertisers who have applied and been approved to advertise those products or services using Google Ads.
For most healthcare policies, if your ad campaign targets allowed locations and the domain is properly certified, your ad will be labeled " Eligible (limited) " and can run in allowed locations.
Below are some examples of healthcare content that is allowed in certain circumstances. You’re expected to familiarize yourself with the local law and regulations for any location your ads target. Learn about what happens if you violate our policies .
Prescription opioid painkillers
Speculative and experimental medical treatment, cell therapies, and gene therapies
Birth control, fertility, and testing
How does this policy differ from location to location?
Google restricts the promotion of services related to the online prescribing, dispensing, and sale of prescription drugs. Businesses subject to this policy include but aren't limited to online pharmacies and telemedicine providers.
Advertisers must apply to serve ads for prescription drug services. Check the location-specific restrictions for every location where you plan to advertise.
Learn more about the Prescription drug services policy.
Google restricts the use of prescription drug terms in ads, landing pages, and keywords.
Depending on location, you may be able to use these terms for the purpose of promoting prescription drugs. Check the location-specific restrictions for every location where you plan to advertise.
Learn more about the Restricted drug terms policy.
Google allows pharmaceutical manufacturers to advertise prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines in select locations only.
Pharmaceutical manufacturers must be certified by Google in order to serve ads.
Learn more about the Pharmaceutical manufacturers policy.
Offering prescription drugs without a prescription is not allowed.
Targeting locations where you aren't licensed is not allowed.
Violations of this policy are taken very seriously and are considered egregious. An egregious violation of the Google Ads policies is a violation so serious that it is unlawful or poses significant harm to our users. In determining whether an advertiser or destination is violating this policy, Google may review information from multiple sources including your ad, website, accounts, and third-party sources. If violations of this policy are found, your Google Ads accounts will be suspended upon detection and without prior warning, and you will not be allowed to advertise with Google Ads again. If you believe there's been an error, and that you haven’t violated our policy, submit an appeal and explain why. Accounts are only reinstated in compelling circumstances, and when there is good reason so it's important that you take the time to be thorough, accurate, and honest. Learn more about suspended accounts .
Learn more about the Unauthorized pharmacies policy.

Portable electric breast pumps
A portable breast pump on this page is an electric breast pump with a built-in battery. You charge it, then pump without a wall socket. These portable electric breast pumps are compact enough for a bag: motor in the cup, or a hospital-strength motor you carry outside the cup.
Portable means battery, so you’re not plugged in while you pump. Every electric breast pump here works that way.
Want the motor in the cup and no tubes? Choose an all-in-one electric. Want the motor off your chest? Choose V1 Pro or V2 Pro.
If you want a tube-free cup in your bra — including hands-free or wireless — go to the Wearable collection . This page stays with electric and portable.
Which electric breast pump is right for you?
There isn’t one best electric breast pump. It depends what you need it for: everyday pumping, a portable kit with a charging case, warmth and massage, or a hospital-strength motor off your chest.
M5 Smart is the everyday electric breast pump for most UK mums: an app, and suction up to −285 mmHg. Start here for a portable electric with a phone app.

Air 1 is the portable electric with a charging case for longer days out, and a 61 mm cup. Choose it if you want extra charge away from a wall socket.

Wellness 1 warms the cup and adds massage with the suction rhythm, with three warmth levels at 37°C, 39°C and 41°C. App control, so you can adjust warmth and massage from your phone.

Hospital-strength, motor off the chest
V1 Pro is the hospital-strength electric if you want the motor off your chest: 15 levels, up to −300 mmHg, for longer sessions at home. V2 Pro is the same type with a 127 g motor if you want a lighter unit.
240 g motor · built-in battery, about 9 sessions · motor in a bag · V2 Pro motor 127 g, under 48 dB
All-in-one electric means the motor sits in the cup, with no tubes. Hospital-strength electric means the motor sits outside. Then check suction, battery, weight, noise and where you carry it.

Electric vs manual breast pumps
Choose an electric breast pump if you pump most days, you’re going back to work, or you want both sides done in one session. A motor does the squeezing for you, and most have a let-down mode then an expression mode, so it takes less time. You pay more, and you charge it.
Choose a manual pump if you only express now and then, or want a quiet spare with no charging. It’s slower if you need a lot of milk every day.
Most electric kits are doubles, so you can express both sides in one session and cut the time. If feeding isn’t going well, speak to your midwife or health visitor.
Bags, bras and a bottle washer
Once you switch the motor off, you still need to store the milk, keep the cups in place, and wash the parts.
Use breast milk storage bags to label and freeze milk flat. Follow NHS guidance on how long milk keeps. A storage jug is useful at home if you prefer to pour milk together before you bag it.
A pumping bra holds the cups in place while you pump. An ordinary stretchy bra can work; a pumping bra is more likely to stay put.
A bottle washer washes and sterilises pump parts in one go, so you’re not facing a sink of parts after every session. It is faster than cleaning breast pump parts by hand. Add a washing block if you want the detergent measured for you.
How to choose a portable electric breast pump
Check the grams if you’ll carry it. M5 Smart is 230 g. Air 1 is 260 g. Wellness 1 is 320 g. V2 Pro’s motor is 127 g if you want the motor off your chest and lighter in a bag.
These charge with USB-C, then run on battery. M5 Smart is about 6 sessions. Air 1’s charging case goes up to 15. Warmth on Wellness 1 uses more battery, about 6 sessions instead of 10.
A double electric kit expresses both sides in one session. Buy a single only if you usually pump one side, or you want a spare. M5 Smart is sold as double or single.
Quieter matters at work or at night. M9 is 42 dB or under. Air 1 and S9 Pro are 45 dB or under. M5 Smart and V2 Pro are under 48 dB.
An all-in-one cup can sit in a bra or go in a bag. On V1 Pro and V2 Pro the motor goes in a bag, off your chest. For a tube-free in-bra pump, including hands-free or wireless, see the Wearable collection .
When you know which type you want, check suction, battery and breast pump price .
What is an electric breast pump?
An electric breast pump uses a motor to express milk, so you’re not squeezing a handle. You can get a portable electric with the motor in the cup, or a hospital-strength pump where the motor sits outside.
Which electric breast pump is best?
There isn’t one best pump for every mum. Most people start with M5 Smart for everyday use. Choose Air 1 if you want a portable kit with a charging case. Choose Wellness 1 if you want in-cup warmth and massage. Choose V1 Pro if you want a stronger motor off your chest.
Is an electric breast pump portable?
Yes. Every electric breast pump on this page has a built-in battery, so you’re not plugged into the wall while you pump. Portable here means battery-powered and compact enough to carry: at home, at work, or out. It is not the same thing as a wearable pump.
Can I use a portable electric pump while travelling?
Yes. Charge it before you leave. A portable electric breast pump runs on its battery, and these kits charge by USB-C from a wall plug, a laptop or a power bank. For several sessions away from a socket, Air 1’s charging case lasts longest on this page, up to 15 sessions. Pack it in your cabin bag and check your airline’s rules for lithium batteries before you fly.
What’s the difference between portable and wearable?
Portable means the pump runs on a battery, so you’re not tied to a socket. Wearable, on this site, means a tube-free in-bra cup, including hands-free and wireless. Those sit on the Wearable collection . A pump can be portable and still be the hospital-strength type, with the motor in a bag rather than in the cup.
What’s the difference between the two types of electric pump?
The difference is where the motor sits. One type has the motor in the cup: no tubes. That’s M5 Smart, Air 1, Wellness 1, M6, M9, S12 Pro Quick and S9 Pro. The other type keeps the motor outside on a short tube. That’s V1 Pro and V2 Pro — hospital-strength, with the motor off your chest. Choose the no-tube type if you want to move around with nothing hanging off you. Choose V1 Pro or V2 Pro if you’d rather keep a stronger motor off your chest.
What is a hospital-strength electric pump?
Hospital-strength means a stronger motor that sits outside, off your chest. On this page that’s V1 Pro and V2 Pro. They are electric pumps you can still carry, with the motor in a bag. If you want a tube-free cup in your bra — including hands-free or wireless — see the Wearable collection.
Should I get an electric or a manual pump?
Go electric if you pump most days, you’re going back to work, or you want both sides done in one go. A manual pump is fine if you only express now and then, and you want something quiet with no charging.
Can I pump both sides at once?
Yes. Most electric kits do both sides together, which is the usual choice if you express from both breasts. A few are also sold as a single — only pick that if you usually pump one side, or you want a spare.
Do I need a pumping bra or storage bags?
You can pump without them, but most mums who express every day end up wanting both. A pumping bra holds the cups in place while you pump. Bags let you label and freeze milk for later.
How should I store expressed milk?
Follow the NHS. They currently say fridge for up to 8 days at 4°C or lower, and freezer at −18°C or lower for up to 6 months. Some NHS pages also allow up to 6 hours at room temperature. Check the NHS expressing page for the latest.
Can an electric pump help with engorgement?
It can take the pressure off if you feel uncomfortably full. If you think you have mastitis, feeding hurts, or baby is not getting milk, talk to your midwife or health visitor.

What is a hands-free breast pump?
In the UK, a hands-free breast pump usually means an in-bra wearable, so you are not holding the flanges. That can be a tube-free all-in-one cup, or collection cups with the motor outside (V1 Pro or V2 Pro). There isn’t one best hands-free pump — match the job in Best for above.
What is a wireless breast pump?
A wireless breast pump, in UK search, usually means an in-bra cup with no wall lead while you pump. Cordless is the same idea. Those pumps sit on this page. Portable means battery-powered electric more broadly — that range is on the Electric collection.
Are V1 Pro and V2 Pro wearable pumps?
Yes. In the UK, wearable usually means the cups sit in your bra. V1 Pro and V2 Pro do that with a separate motor unit and in-bra collection cups. They are not all-in-one, tube-free wearables like M5 Smart or Air 1. Shop hospital-strength electric pumps if you want that format in more depth.
How should I store expressed milk in the UK?
Follow current NHS guidance. The NHS advises storing expressed milk in the fridge for up to 8 days at 4°C or lower, and in a freezer at −18°C or lower for up to 6 months. Some NHS pages also allow up to 6 hours at room temperature. Check the NHS expressing page before you rely on a figure.
Measure nipple diameter, not bra cup. Most Momcozy wearables include 17/19/21 mm inserts with a 24 mm flange. Pain, a white ring on the nipple, or too much areola being pulled in means resize before you turn suction up. Fit matters more than buying a “stronger” pump.
Do wearable pumps decrease milk supply?
Not if the cup empties the breast well. Supply drops when the seal is poor, the flange is the wrong size, or sessions are too short or too infrequent — not because the motor sits in the bra. If output falls, check fit first, then session length. Speak to a midwife or lactation specialist if you’re worried about supply.
Can I exclusively use a wearable breast pump?
Yes, if it empties you comfortably and your output stays steady. Plenty of UK mums use an all-in-one wearable as their only pump. If you need longer sessions at home with the motor off the chest, V1 Pro and V2 Pro are on this page; the wider hospital-strength electric range is on the Electric collection.
Can I wear a regular bra while pumping?
A stretchy everyday bra can hold a cup if it is supportive enough to keep the seal. A dedicated pumping bra is more reliable for leaks and for leaning forward a little. If milk escapes, it is usually fit or angle, not a reason to jump model.
Does warmth and massage in a wearable pump help with let-down?
Some mums find in-cup warmth and a massage rhythm easier at the start of a session. Wellness 1 warms to 37°C, 39°C or 41°C. Warmth uses more battery — about 6 sessions with warmth, about 10 pumping only. It is a comfort feature, not a medical treatment. Speak to a midwife or lactation specialist if pumping is painful.

What is an ultra slim breast pump?
An ultra slim breast pump is a wearable, in-bra cup with a thinner profile than a typical all-in-one, so it sits flatter under clothes. Air 1 is 61 mm — built for UK mums who express at work or away from home and do not want a bulky outline. A slim breast pump is about how it sits, not about being the quietest motor.
What makes Air 1 different from other slim wearable breast pumps?
Air 1 is Momcozy’s slimmest all-in-one wearable at 61 mm, about 22% slimmer than M9. You get a transparent top to centre the nipple, a 180 ml collector, and a charging case for up to 15 sessions. Choose it when a lower in-bra profile is the job. If a quieter motor matters more than how slim the cup sits, M9 is the better match.
Is the Air 1 ultra slim breast pump good for pumping at work?
Yes. That is the job it is built for. The 61 mm cup sits in a nursing bra under work clothes, so you can keep pumping at work without a bulky outline. The charging case covers a run of sessions away from a plug. If a shared room means noise matters more than profile, choose M9.
Is the Momcozy Air 1 easy to use for first-time mums?
Yes. The transparent top lets you see the nipple is centred before you start — usually the hardest step on a wearable. There are five parts to wash, buttons on the cup, and the app only if you want it. You can express without opening your phone.
How do I use the Air 1 ultra-slim breast pump?
Wash and assemble the five milk-contact parts. Keep the motor dry.
Place the cup in your bra. Use the transparent top to centre the nipple in the tunnel.
Turn on. Choose Stimulation, Expression or Mixed on the cup or in the app, then pick a suction level that feels comfortable — not the highest.
When the 180 ml collector is full, the app can alert you. Switch off, take the motor off, then pour.
How do I centre the flange on the Air 1?
Look through the transparent top and check the nipple sits in the middle of the tunnel, not pulled to one side. Measure nipple diameter, not bra cup. Air 1 ships with a 24 mm flange and 17/19/21 mm inserts. Pain, a white ring, or too much areola being pulled in means resize before you turn suction up.
Can I track expressing sessions and milk volume?
Yes. The Momcozy app can switch modes, show milk volume as you go, alert you when the collector is full, and keep a session history. The pump still runs from the buttons on the cup if you would rather not use the phone.
How long does the Air 1 charging case last?
The case holds enough power for up to 15 sessions of about 30 minutes. Seat each pump so the contacts line up; the case tops them up and stores them for a work day or a few days out. Charge the case from a plug at home, then take it with you.
How do I clean and sterilise the Air 1 ultra-slim breast pump?
Take the motor off first and wipe it dry only — never soak it. Rinse the five milk-contact parts (collector, back cover, flange, valve, diaphragm) straight after use, wash in warm soapy water, then sterilise with steam or a cold-water method. Air-dry fully before you assemble.

Is Momcozy M9 hospital-grade breast pump?
Momcozy M9 is a wearable, personal breast pump with hospital-grade suction power . It is helpful to know the distinction between a "hospital-grade" pump and "hospital-grade suction."
A "hospital-grade" breast pump is a multi-use, rental pump designed for use in a hospital or clinical settings. They are made in a closed system so the milk won't get into the motor or tubing, so they can be shared with many mothers safely. They are most commonly for mums who need to establish their milk supply or mums with a baby in the NICU.
On the other hand, "hospital-grade suction power" refers to the suction power and cycle rate of the pump. This is used to refer to a pump that can produce sufficient suction to initiate and maintain a milk supply by mimicking a powerful suckling baby.
Brief and to the point, the Momcozy M9 delivers powerful performance in a convenient, hands-free configuration that's perfect for personal, in-your-home or on-the-go applications. Unless you have a medical need for a multi-user pump, a personal pump with hospital-grade suction like the M9 should be ample power for your daily pumping needs.

A wearable pump does not decrease milk supply, as long as it provides strong and effective suction. Suction strength is key to fully emptying the breast, which helps maintain a healthy milk supply.

Yes, you can exclusively pump with a hands-free breast pump. In fact, many moms find hands-free pumping to be a convenient and effective way to build and maintain milk supply, especially when nursing isn’t an option.

Is It Good to Use Electric Breast Pumps?
Yes. Electric breast pumps are a great choice for breastfeeding mums looking for convenience and efficiency. They can help maintain or increase milk supply, especially for working mothers or those with low supply issues. Choosing the right electric breast pump means finding one that offers strong suction power, quiet operation, and easy-to-use features. A comfortable and effective electric breast pump can make your breastfeeding journey smoother and more successful.
How Many Minutes Should I Use an Electric Breast Pump?
For most mums, starting with 15–20 minutes per pumping session is recommended, gradually adjusting based on your milk supply and comfort. Everyone's needs are different, so listen to your body and pump according to what feels best for you.
Factors like your milk production, your baby’s feeding schedule, and your comfort all play a role. Stop pumping if you feel any discomfort or when your breasts feel empty to avoid over-pumping, which can cause soreness or irritation. Using your electric breast pump correctly helps maintain a healthy milk supply and a comfortable breastfeeding experience.
Do Wearable Pumps Decrease Milk Supply?
A wearable pump does not decrease milk supply, as long as it provides strong and effective suction. Suction strength is key to fully emptying the breast, which helps maintain a healthy milk supply.
Wearable pumps like the Momcozy S12 Pro are designed with high suction power to ensure efficient milk removal, so you can pump hands-free without compromising your milk production.
Which Is Less Painful: Manual or Electric Breast Pump?
Pain during pumping varies from mum to mum, but many breastfeeding mothers find electric breast pumps to be less painful because they offer multiple adjustable suction levels and modes, allowing you to customise comfort and reduce nipple pain. However, using too high suction, especially with sensitive nipples or elastic nipples, can still cause discomfort.
Some mums prefer manual breast pumps because they provide more control over suction and pumping speed, which can help minimise pain. Yet, manual pumps may cause hand and wrist fatigue when used for long sessions.
Regardless of whether you choose a manual or electric breast pump, selecting the right breast pump flange size and adjusting the suction level correctly are essential for reducing pain, preventing nipple soreness, and ensuring a comfortable pumping experience.
How Do I Choose an Electric Breast Pump?
Choosing the right electric breast pump can make all the difference for busy mums. Here are key factors to consider:
Portability: If you pump on the go or at work, choose a lightweight, portable breast pump like the Momcozy M6 that fits your lifestyle.
Suction Power: Look for a pump with strong and adjustable suction to effectively express milk and maintain a healthy milk supply.
Comfort: The right fit matters, so try different pumps and flanges to find one that feels comfortable and prevents nipple pain or discomfort.
Features: Consider useful features such as double pumping for efficiency, quiet operation for discretion, rechargeable batteries for convenience, and app control for personalised pumping sessions.
Picking the right electric breast pump tailored to your needs helps make breastfeeding easier, more comfortable, and more efficient.
How should I clean and sterilize M6 accessories?
Wash M6 accessories with regular dish soap. If sterilisation is needed, boil them for 5 minutes, then air dry, wipe dry, or use low-temperature drying. Do not use microwave sterilisation. For steam sterilising, drying, or hot-air drying, keep the temperature within 100°C / 212°F when possible and do not exceed 110°C / 230°F. M6 accessories can also be cleaned in a Momcozy bottle washer, but please do not use Storage mode. Avoid alcohol-based cleaners, as they may affect the soft silicone on the flange.
Why does the suction feel weaker after cleaning or sterilizing?
Suction may feel weaker if the milk collector or flange is slightly deformed after excessive heat exposure, which can affect the airtight seal. Please check whether the accessories are fully dry, properly installed, and free from warping, gaps, or damage. To help maintain strong suction, avoid microwave sterilisation and keep steam sterilising, drying, or hot-air drying within the recommended temperature range.

Is V1 Pro a wearable breast pump?
Yes — in the UK sense. Wearable usually means the cups sit in your bra so you can move around. V1 Pro does that with a separate motor unit and in-bra collection cups, on a short tube. It is not an all-in-one, tube-free wearable like M5 Smart or Air 1.
What is a hospital-strength electric breast pump with in-bra cups?
It is an electric breast pump where the motor stays off your chest and the cups go in your bra. Hands-free here means you are not holding the flanges — it is not the same as a tube-free cup. V1 Pro is that format: 15 suction levels and up to −300 mmHg, for UK mums who want a stronger motor at home. We do not call it hospital-grade.
Is V1 Pro a good electric breast pump for home?
Yes. Choose V1 Pro when you want longer sessions at home with the motor off your chest, 15 levels, and cups that still sit in the bra. It is a strong electric breast pump if emptying well matters more than having no tubes. If you want everything in the bra and no tubing, start with M5 Smart.
What is the difference between V1 Pro and V2 Pro?
Same type: separate unit, in-bra cups, tubing. V1 Pro has more levels (15) and suction up to −300 mmHg, with a 240 g motor — the home, more-control pick. V2 Pro is the lighter unit: 127 g motor, nine levels, up to −288 mmHg. Pick V1 Pro for finer control; pick V2 Pro if you want the motor easier to carry.
Should I get V1 Pro or an all-in-one like M5 Smart?
If you want the whole pump in your bra with no tubes, choose M5 Smart (or Air 1 / M9). If you would rather keep a stronger motor off your chest and still have in-bra cups, choose V1 Pro. Hands-free is true of both; the split is where the motor sits.
Assemble each cup: flange, collector and valve. Keep the motor dry.
Seat the cups in a pumping bra. Use the inserts so the nipple sits centred in the tunnel.
Clip or pocket the motor and connect the tubes. Choose a rhythm and a suction level that feels comfortable — not the highest.
When you finish, switch off, disconnect the tubes, then pour.
Measure nipple diameter, not bra cup. V1 Pro includes a 24 mm DoubleFit flange and 17/19/21 mm inserts. Pain, a white ring, or too much areola being pulled in means resize before you turn suction up. Fit empties the breast better than chasing a higher number.
How do I clean and sterilise V1 Pro?
Wipe the motor dry only — never soak it or the tubing ends on the motor. Wash the three milk-contact parts per cup (flange, collector, valve) in warm soapy water, then sterilise with steam or a cold-water method. Air-dry fully. Follow current NHS guidance when you store expressed milk.

Mega Produkt! Die bessere Wahl für Vielpumpen und maximale Diskretion
Die Momcozy Air 1 Ultra-Slim ist bei uns im Einsatz und wird direkt mit der bereits bekannten Momcozy M5 verglichen. Beide Pumpen haben ihre Berechtigung, sprechen aber klar unterschiedliche Nutzungsszenarien an. Bewertet wird hier die Air 1, der Vergleich zur M5 dient der Einordnung. Meine Frau nutzt die Pumpe im Alltag parallel zur Betreuung von Theo, der gerade zwei Jahre alt ist. Das bedeutet Bewegung, Termine, Alltag, nicht still sitzen am Sofa. Genau hier zeigt sich sehr schnell, ob eine tragbare Milchpumpe wirklich alltagstauglich ist oder nur auf dem Papier. Die größte Stärke der Air 1 ist ihre Bauform. Sie ist deutlich flacher als die M5 und trägt im BH sichtbar weniger auf. Unter normaler Kleidung fällt sie kaum auf. Im direkten Vergleich wirkt die M5 eher wie eine Kugel, die Air 1 wie ein integriertes Bauteil. Gerade unterwegs, im Auto oder bei Terminen ist das ein echter Unterschied. Diskretion ist hier kein Marketingbegriff, sondern real spürbar. Auch technisch spielt die Air 1 in einer anderen Liga. Die Saugkraft ist spürbar stärker und feiner regelbar. Mit bis zu 15 Intensitätsstufen und mehreren Modi lässt sich das Pumpen sehr genau anpassen. Während die M5 für gelegentliches bis mittleres Pumpen völlig ausreicht, merkt man bei häufiger Nutzung, dass die Air 1 konstanter arbeitet. Gerade bei längeren Sessions oder höherer Milchmenge wirkt sie weniger angestrengt. Ein klarer Mehrwert gegenüber der M5 ist die App Anbindung. Die Steuerung per App, das Tracking der Sessions und vor allem der Echtzeit Füllstandssensor machen den Alltag einfacher. Die Warnung bei vollem Behälter verhindert Überlaufen und erspart ständiges Kontrollieren. Das klingt nach Spielerei, ist im Alltag aber tatsächlich sehr hilfreich. Das kabellose Ladecase ist ein weiterer Punkt, der die Air 1 klar absetzt. Während die M5 klassisch per USB geladen wird und an Steckdosen gebunden ist, kann die Air 1 unterwegs einfach im Case nachgeladen werden. Für Tage mit viel Bewegung oder längeren Terminen ist das ein echter Vorteil. Mobilität wird hier ernst genommen. Die Milchbehälter fassen 180 ml pro Seite und sind damit auch für höhere Milchmengen geeignet. Für Nutzerinnen mit hoher Fördermenge oder häufigem Pumpen ist das wichtig. Die Entleerung ist gut, die transparente Abdeckung erleichtert die korrekte Positionierung. Es gibt aber auch Nachteile. Die Air 1 ist teurer als die M5 und dieser Aufpreis lohnt sich nicht für jede Nutzung. Wer nur gelegentlich pumpt oder eine Zweitpumpe sucht, fährt mit der M5 preislich besser. Zudem berichten einige Nutzerinnen von Verarbeitungsproblemen nach längerer Nutzung, insbesondere am Motor oder am Ladecase. Das konnten wir bisher nicht feststellen, bleibt aber ein Punkt, den man im Hinterkopf haben sollte. Auch die Flange könnte für manche etwas weicher oder flexibler sein. Hier ist manchmal Nachjustieren nötig, bis der Sitz perfekt passt. Im direkten Vergleich lässt sich das Fazit klar ziehen. Die M5 ist eine gute, solide Alltagspumpe mit fairer Preis Leistung, ideal für gelegentliche bis mittlere Nutzung. Die Air 1 Ultra-Slim ist die konsequentere Lösung für Vielpumpen, für maximale Diskretion und für Nutzerinnen, die technische Unterstützung und Mobilität wirklich nutzen. Für unseren Alltag mit Kleinkind, Bewegung und wenig Stillstand ist die Air 1 die bessere Wahl. Sie ist kein Schnäppchen, aber ein durchdachtes Werkzeug, das den Alltag spürbar erleichtert.

Parto col dire che sono al mi terzo figlio, dono il latte alla banca del latte per quanto ne ho in eccesso, per me un buco tiralatte elettrico è vitale.
Ho acquistato il tiralatte prima del parto perché in offerta, prima di questo ne ho avuti diversi, dal più classico avent manuale al precedente medela a mani libere ad un prezzo allora enorme.
Con questi due mi sto trovando benissimo, anche se ci sono alcuni difetti migliorabile.
Sono comodi, senza fili in mezzo, le impostazioni di estrazione sono comode e da app possono esserne create di personali.
È molto confortevole e possiede già ogni misura di flangia per il seno.
Ciò che andrebbe migliorato riguarda i pezzi, sono diversi, montarlo e smontarlo è abbastanza lungo, soprattutto se il tiralatte va usato più di una volta al giorno, e bisogna fare coincidere bene tutti i pezzi perché altrimenti ci possono essere perdite o non entrare in vuoto.
La mancanza di un display integrato ti obbliga ad avere sempre un occhio l'app e la misurazione del latte non è sempre precisissima.
Sarebbe comoda anche una piccola illuminazione per poter usare senza molta luce il tiralatte.
Nel complesso è un prodotto che uso bene, che non mi ha dato problemi o difetti, ma che, soprattutto visto il prezzo al netto di promozioni o sconti, potrebbe e dovrebbe essere migliorato, per renderlo perfetto.
Avrei acquistato di nuovo medela, che a pari prodotto (ma con recensioni più basse) ha visto impennare i tiralatte di molto, a fronte di ancor più difetti, quindi non ho un vero comparativo con altri indossabile se non appunto il precedente uso di medela handsfree.
Come si dice, visto il prezzo fallo pure andare male, per questo do una stella in meno: al prezzo di vendita non posso esserci difetti!

Good sleep is essential for our health and emotional well-being.
Getting enough sleep and good sleep quality are essential for healthy sleep.
The amount of sleep you need changes as you age.
Talk to your healthcare provider if you have problems sleeping.
The daily recommended hours of sleep you need changes as you age.

Getting enough sleep can help you:
Reduce stress and improve your mood.
Improve your heart health and metabolism.
Lower your risk of chronic conditions like:
Lessen the risk of motor vehicle crashes and related injury or death.
Improve your attention and memory to better perform daily activities.
Better sleep habits can help you get a good night's sleep. Habits that can improve your sleep include:
Going to bed and getting up at the same time every day.
Keeping your bedroom quiet, relaxing, and at a cool temperature.
Turning off electronic devices at least 30 minutes before bedtime.
Avoiding large meals and alcohol before bedtime.
Avoiding caffeine in the afternoon or evening.
Exercising regularly and maintaining a healthy diet.
Quality sleep means you are getting uninterrupted and refreshing sleep. Getting quality sleep is not just about how many hours you sleep, but how well you sleep.
Signs of poor sleep quality include:
Repeatedly waking up during the night.
Feeling sleepy or tired even after getting enough sleep.

Maybe you saw those words on a company’s website or in an ad promoting a product or treatment. Some marketers may say their products are “FDA approved.” How can you know for sure what the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved?
The FDA is responsible for protecting public health by regulating human drugs and biological products, animal drugs, medical devices, tobacco products, food (including animal food), cosmetics, and electronic products that emit radiation.
But not all those products undergo premarket approval – that is, a review of safety, quality, and effectiveness by FDA experts and agency approval before a product can be sold to consumers. In some cases, the FDA’s statutory authority means that the agency needs to focus on products after they are already for sale. That is determined by Congress in establishing the FDA’s authorities . Here is a guide to how the FDA regulates products — and what the agency does (and doesn’t) approve.
The FDA doesn’t approve health care providers.
The FDA does not “approve” health care providers, including physician offices or laboratories. The FDA does have authority to inspect regulated facilities to verify that they comply with certain legal requirements that can affect the safety or quality of products produced or stored in those facilities.
Although manufacturing facilities and contract manufacturers are often inspected as part of a product application for certain products that require premarket approval, and such facilities are frequently required to register, the agency does not approve manufacturing facilities independently. The FDA inspects regulated facilities to verify they comply with applicable current good manufacturing practices and other requirements, including an adequately designed and controlled production process.
Unless an exemption applies (like domestic manufacturing facilities), drug, foreign food, and most device facilities must register with the FDA before exporting products to the U.S. Mere registration of an establishment or listing of a drug or device does not denote approval of the establishment, the drug or device, or other drugs or devices of the establishment, nor does it mean that a product may be legally marketed.
Mammography facilities must be certified by the FDA, or by a state that has received FDA approval as a certifier and must display their FDA certificates where patients can see them. A mammography facility that receives Mammography Quality Standards Act (MQSA) certification has shown it is capable of providing quality mammography.
The FDA approves new human drugs and biological products.
With rare exceptions, new drugs and biological products for people must be FDA approved before they are marketed, offered for sale, or shipped in interstate commerce. This means a company must demonstrate that its drug or biological product is safe and effective for the intended use and that it can manufacture the product to federal quality standards. If the FDA grants an approval, it means the agency has determined the benefits of a drug outweigh the risks for the intended use, or that a biological product is safe, pure, and potent.
Some examples of biological products that require approval are therapeutic proteins, vaccines, allergenic products, cellular and gene therapies, and products manufactured from plasma. Manufacturers must also prove they are able to make the drug or biological product according to federal quality standards.
The FDA also approves generic drugs and biosimilar medications for patient use. Biosimilars and generics are FDA-approved medicines that increase access to treatment options at potentially more affordable prices through increased competition with innovator medications.
The FDA does not develop products before approving them. Instead, FDA experts conduct a careful evaluation of the results of laboratory, animal, and human clinical testing done by manufacturers. The FDA does perform lot release testing of certain biological products, which provides the agency with a real-time system to continuously monitor product quality, through review and testing.

A complete list of licensed biological products and establishments.

The FDA doesn’t approve compounded drugs.
Compounding is generally a practice in which a licensed pharmacist, a licensed physician, or, in the case of an outsourcing facility, a person under the supervision of a licensed pharmacist, combines, mixes, or alters ingredients of a drug to create medications that meet the needs of individual patients, including those who are allergic to ingredients in FDA-approved medicines or who cannot swallow an FDA-approved pill.
Although they can be important parts of America’s health care system, compounded drugs are not FDA approved. By statute, compounders do not need to prove to the FDA that their products meet the same standards that drug manufacturers need to meet. This means that the FDA does not conduct premarket review for compounded drugs to evaluate their safety, effectiveness, or quality.
The FDA uses a risk-based, tiered approach for regulating medical devices for people.
The FDA classifies medical devices according to risk and the level of regulatory controls needed to provide a reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the devices. The highest-risk devices (Class III), such as mechanical heart valves and implantable infusion pumps, generally require FDA approval of a premarket approval application before marketing. To receive FDA approval for these devices, manufacturers must demonstrate with sufficient, valid scientific evidence that there is a reasonable assurance that the devices are safe and effective for their intended uses.
Generally, manufacturers of moderate-risk medical devices (Class II) (for example dialysis equipment and many types of catheters) may market such devices pursuant to so-called “510(k) clearance,” allowing distribution once the manufacturer has demonstrated that the device is substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate device that does not require premarket approval. Class II devices are subject to general controls and can also be subject to special controls. Special controls may include specific testing or labeling requirements for that device.
Devices that are low risk of harm to the user (Class I) – for example non-powered breast pumps, elastic bandages, tongue depressors, and exam gloves – are subject to general controls only. Most are exempt from premarket notification requirements.
The FDA uses a risk-based approach for human cells and tissues.
All human cells and tissues intended for use in people — collectively referred to as human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps) — are regulated to prevent the transmission of infectious disease. Examples of HCT/Ps include bone, skin, corneas, ligaments, tendons, dura mater, heart valves, and reproductive tissue.
Those HCT/Ps that pose an additional risk because of their processing or use also require FDA approval before marketing.
The FDA does not regulate the transplantation of vascularized human organ transplants such as kidney, liver, heart, lung, or pancreas. The Health Resources Services Administration oversees the transplantation of vascularized human organs.
The FDA doesn’t approve tobacco products.
There’s no such thing as a safe tobacco product. By statute, the FDA’s safe and effective standard for evaluating medical products does not apply to tobacco products. Instead, the FDA regulates tobacco products based on a public health standard that considers the product’s risks and benefits to the population as a whole, including users and non-users of the tobacco product.
To legally sell, market, manufacture, or distribute a new tobacco product in the U.S., an applicant must receive authorization from the FDA. There are three pathways available to bring a new tobacco product to market: premarket tobacco product applications, substantial equivalence applications, and exemption from substantial equivalence requests .
A marketing authorization does not indicate that the tobacco product is safe or “FDA approved,” and many marketed tobacco products are not actually being legally sold. Rather, the issuance of a marketing authorization means that the applicant has complied with the requirements under the law to bring its product to market. The FDA lists all authorized tobacco products in its Searchable Tobacco Products Database .
The FDA approves food additives.
Although the FDA does not approve food products, certain ingredients must be approved by the FDA before they are used in food or in materials that contact food. Those include food additives (certain substances added intentionally to food, as well as certain substances that migrate to food from food contact products such as food packaging), and color additives, unless they are subject to an exception, such as the “generally recognized as safe” (GRAS) exception.
Companies that want to add new food additives to food are responsible for providing the FDA with information demonstrating that the additives are safe. FDA experts review the information submitted by companies, as well as other available safety data and information, to determine whether the food additive is safe for its intended use. An approved food additive must be used in compliance with its approved uses, specifications, and restrictions.
Certain food ingredients, such as those that are GRAS by scientific experts under their conditions of intended use, do not require premarket approval by the FDA. The FDA has a voluntary notification process under which a manufacturer may submit a conclusion that the use of an ingredient is GRAS.
The FDA approves color additives used in FDA-regulated products.
This includes those used in food (including animal food), dietary supplements, drugs, cosmetics, and some medical devices. These color additives (except coal-tar hair dyes) are subject by law to approval by the agency before market entry, and each must be used only in compliance with its approved uses, specifications, and restrictions.
In the approval process, the FDA evaluates safety data to ensure that a color additive is safe for its intended purposes.
The FDA doesn’t approve cosmetics.
Cosmetics must be safe for their intended use and properly labeled.
Examples of cosmetics include perfumes, makeup, moisturizers, shampoos, hair dyes, face and body cleansers, and shaving preparations. Cosmetic products and ingredients, and their labeling, do not require FDA approval. There’s one exception: color additives (other than coal-tar hair dyes), which need to be approved by the FDA for their use.
The FDA generally doesn’t approve medical foods.
A medical food is formulated to be consumed or administered enterally under the supervision of a physician and is intended for the specific dietary management of a disease or condition for which distinctive nutritional requirements, based on recognized scientific principles, are established by medical evaluation. An example of a disease or condition that a medical food could be used to manage is phenylketonuria, a genetic disorder. Someone with this disorder may need medical foods that are formulated to be free of the amino acid phenylalanine.
Medical foods do not include products such as meal replacements or diet shakes, or products for the management of diseases that can be managed through modification of the normal diet alone.
Medical foods do not undergo premarket approval by the FDA. Still, medical food companies must comply with other requirements, such as current good manufacturing practice and registration of food facilities. Medical foods do not have to include a Nutrition Facts label on their labels. But any statements on their label or in other labeling must be truthful and not misleading.
The FDA doesn’t approve infant formula, but infant formula is heavily regulated.
The FDA does not approve infant formulas before they can be marketed. But new infant formulas are subject to a premarket review by the FDA, and the FDA can object to product or ingredient being notified.
Manufacturers must ensure that their infant formula complies with federal nutrient and safety requirements and other regulations. Manufacturers must register all establishments at which they intend to manufacture new infant formula and provide the agency with a new infant formula submission at least 90 days before marketing a new formula. The FDA reviews the information in the submission for safety, nutritional adequacy, and to evaluate compliance with other important requirements. Both infant formulas and manufacturers of infant formula are subject to the FDA’s regulatory oversight.
The FDA conducts at least yearly inspections of all facilities, including new ones, that manufacture infant formula and collects and analyzes product samples. If the FDA determines that an infant formula that has left the control of the manufacturer may not provide all required nutrients or is otherwise adulterated or misbranded, and that such formula presents a risk to human health, the manufacturer of the formula must conduct a recall. Examples of an adulterated infant formula include a formula that contains less than the minimum required amount of a nutrient, or a formula contaminated with bacteria that can make an infant sick.
The FDA doesn’t approve dietary supplements.
By statute, the FDA does not approve dietary supplements for safety and effectiveness. In fact, many dietary supplements can be marketed without even notifying the FDA.
Dietary supplement companies must ensure their products are safe and comply with other labeling and quality requirements, such as good manufacturing practices. Also, companies are required to submit a premarket safety notification to the FDA at least 75 days before marketing dietary supplements containing certain “new dietary ingredients” (that were not marketed in the U.S. before Oct. 15, 1994).
The FDA inspects facilities for compliance and monitors adverse event reports. When public health concerns arise about the safety of a dietary supplement or an ingredient, the FDA has the authority to take action to protect the public.
The FDA doesn’t approve a product’s food label, including its Nutrition Facts label.
The FDA does not approve individual labels before food products, including dietary supplements, can be marketed. But FDA regulations require specific labeling elements, including nutrition information, to appear on most foods, including dietary supplements. Also, any statements on food products must be truthful and not misleading – and must comply with any regulatory requirements for the type of statement, as applicable.
Manufacturers must provide the serving size of the food and specified information about the nutrient content of each serving on the Nutrition Facts label (or on the Supplement Facts label for dietary supplements).
The FDA generally doesn’t approve structure-function claims on dietary supplements and other foods.
Structure-function claims describe the role of a food, including dietary supplement, or food component (such as a nutrient) that is intended to affect the structure or function of the human body. One example is “calcium builds strong bones.”
Dietary supplement companies that make structure-function claims on labels or in other labeling must submit a notification to the FDA. Structure-function claims on dietary supplements carry a disclaimer stating that the claim has not been evaluated by the FDA, and that the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.
Conventional food manufacturers are not required to notify the agency about structure-function claims associated with their products or to include a disclaimer. By law, all such claims must be truthful and not misleading.
The misuse of the FDA’s logo may violate federal law.
The FDA’s logo is for official government use only. The FDA’s logo should not be used to misrepresent the agency or to suggest that the FDA endorses any private organization, product, or service.
These are just some of the many ways the FDA is responsible for protecting the public health.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is issuing this guidance document to provide clarity to industry and FDA staff on the Center for Devices and Radiological Health's (CDRH's) compliance policy for low risk products that promote a healthy lifestyle (general wellness products). 1 This guidance does not apply to products (e.g., drugs, biologics, dietary supplements, foods, or cosmetics) regulated by other FDA Centers or to combination products. 2
Section 3060(a) of the 21st Century Cures Act (Cures Act) amended section 520 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) on December 13, 2016, removing certain software functions, including those intended for maintaining or encouraging a healthy lifestyle that are unrelated to the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, prevention, or treatment of a disease or condition, from the definition of device in section 201(h) of the FD&C Act. Section 520(o)(1)(B) of the FD&C Act, states that software that is intended "for maintaining or encouraging a healthy lifestyle and is unrelated to the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, prevention, or treatment of a disease or condition" is not a device under section 201(h) of the FD&C Act.
This guidance clarifies FDA's interpretation of this provision and its application to general wellness products.
1 This guidance does not change or rescind any requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) or any applicable regulations. 2 For determinations on combination products, contact the Office of Combination Products at combination@fda.gov . See 21 CFR 3.2(e) for the definition of a combination product.

Health Products Compliance Guidance
Federal Trade Commission (FTC) staff has prepared this guidance document to update and replace Dietary Supplements: An Advertising Guide for Industry , issued in 1998. Like the 1998 guide, this document provides guidance from FTC staff on how to ensure that claims about the benefits and safety of health-related products are truthful, not misleading, and supported by science. Since 1998, the FTC has settled or adjudicated more than 200 cases involving false or misleading advertising claims about the benefits or safety of dietary supplements or other health-related products, including foods, over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, homeopathic products, health equipment, diagnostic tests, and health-related apps. This update draws on the issues raised in those cases to illustrate how the FTC identifies the express and implied claims conveyed in advertising and how the agency evaluates the scientific support for those claims. While most of the examples involve dietary supplement advertising, the same legal principles apply to the marketing of any health-related product.
This document is intended as business guidance only. It interprets and explains FTC advertising law pursuant to the FTC Act and as set out in case law, and Commission policy statements. The guide, however, doesn’t have the force or effect of law. The principles and examples are intended to help advertisers comply with the basic tenets of FTC law. They don’t provide a safe harbor from potential liability; whether a particular advertising claim is deceptive or otherwise violates the FTC Act will depend on the facts of the specific case.
II. Overview of Regulatory Framework
A. FTC Authority over Advertising of Health-Related Products
The Federal Trade Commission’s broad mandate is to prevent “unfair or deceptive acts or practices.” That includes making sure the information marketers provide about the benefits and safety of dietary supplements and other health-related products is accurate so consumers can make informed decisions. Sections 5 and 12 of the FTC Act, [1] along with the FTC’s policy statements on deception and advertising substantiation , [2] are the foundation of FTC truth-in-advertising law, and can be distilled down to two common-sense principles:
1) Advertising must be truthful and not misleading; and
2) Before disseminating an ad, advertisers must have adequate substantiation for all objective product claims conveyed, expressly or by implication, to consumers acting reasonably.
A deceptive ad is one that contains a material misrepresentation or omission that is likely to mislead consumers acting reasonably under the circumstances. The type of substantiation needed for a claim depends on many factors, including the product being marketed and the nature of the claim. As a general rule, however, claims about the health benefits or safety of foods, dietary supplements, drugs, and other health-related products require substantiation in the form of competent and reliable scientific evidence. [3]
“Advertising” refers to a wide variety of marketing techniques . The term “advertising” as used throughout this guide refers not only to traditional TV, radio, print, and internet ads, but also more broadly to the variety of marketing techniques and promotion methods that marketers engage in to increase consumer interest in, or demand for, their products. Thus, as used here, advertising includes statements or depictions on packaging and labeling; in promotional materials such as brochures or booklets; on the internet and in other digital content; in social media and influencer marketing; in press releases, press interviews, or other media appearances; at trade shows, conferences, and seminars; and indirectly through healthcare practitioners or other intermediaries. [4] Promotional product information distributed through any of these means must comply with the same truth-in-advertising principles that apply to traditional ads. [5]
Anyone participating in deceptive marketing is potentially liable under FTC law. Marketers of dietary supplements and other health-related products should ensure that anyone participating in marketing is familiar with basic FTC advertising principles. All parties who participate directly in marketing and promotion, or who have authority to control those practices, have an obligation to make sure that claims are presented truthfully and to check the adequacy of the support for those claims. The FTC has taken action not just against product marketers, but also, in appropriate circumstances, against individual owners and corporate officers of the marketer, as well as ad agencies, distributors, retailers, catalog companies, infomercial producers, expert endorsers, and others engaged in deceptive marketing and promotion. [6]
The FTC can seek a variety of remedies for deceptive advertising. The consequences of deceiving consumers about the safety, efficacy, or other benefits of a product can be substantial. The FTC can obtain an order that stops the deceptive claims and requires that future marketing be truthful and substantiated. In appropriate circumstances, the FTC also can mandate certain disclosures or require that a marketer engage in corrective advertising to cure any lingering deception in the marketplace. [7] In particularly egregious instances, the FTC has asked a court to ban a company or individual from engaging in certain marketing activities altogether. [8] The FTC also can seek financial remedies, including, in some instances, consumer refunds or civil penalties.
The FTC and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) share jurisdiction over the marketing of dietary supplements, foods, drugs, devices, and other health-related products. The agencies coordinate their enforcement and regulatory efforts pursuant to a Memorandum of Understanding – often called the “FDA-FTC Liaison Agreement” – that governs the basic division of responsibilities between them. [9] The FDA has primary responsibility for claims that appear in labeling , including the package, product inserts, and other promotional materials available at point of sale. The FTC has primary responsibility for claims in all forms of advertising . [10] Because of this shared jurisdiction, the two agencies work closely to ensure that their enforcement efforts are consistent to the fullest extent feasible. Marketers should be aware that the FDA/FTC Liaison Agreement doesn’t limit the FTC’s jurisdiction or prohibit the agency from taking action against deceptive labeling claims or obtaining orders that address all forms of marketing, including claims that appear in labeling.
C. Key Differences Between FTC and FDA Law
While both the FTC and the FDA require marketing of dietary supplements and other health-related products to be truthful and accurate, there are some key differences in the agencies’ legal frameworks and approaches that marketers should keep in mind.
FTC advertising law applies to all products and claims. Unlike FDA law, FTC law makes no bright-line distinctions between categories of health-related products or claims. For example, provisions in the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA) regarding “structure/function” claims [11] in labeling don’t govern the FTC’s assessment of those claims in advertising. [12] The FTC follows the same basic steps when evaluating any health-related claim regardless of whether, under FDA law, the claim would be considered a health claim, a structure/function claim, or a drug claim. Similarly, the FTC’s approach to advertising of health-related products is the same regardless of whether, under FDA law, the product is considered a food, a supplement, or a drug. [13]
The FTC doesn’t pre-approve “health” claims, as that term is defined by FDA labeling laws. The FTC Act doesn’t require pre-market approval of health claims in the advertising of foods, dietary supplements, or other products. Marketers should be aware, however, that the FTC gives great deference to a determination by the FDA of whether there is adequate support for a particular health claim in labeling. Health claims that meet the FDA “significant scientific agreement” standard will be presumed to be substantiated under FTC law. [14] Health claims that do not meet the FDA’s “significant scientific agreement” standard may be deceptive unless the limitations or uncertainty in the supporting science are clearly communicated with qualifying language that is noticed and understood by consumers. [15] Sections III.A.3 and III.B.5 below provide more detailed guidance on the clear and conspicuous disclosure of such limitations for claims based on emerging science.
The FTC doesn’t require notification for “structure/function” claims. Under FDA labeling law, dietary supplement marketers must notify the FDA of structure/function claims and other statements of nutritional support that appear in labeling, but don’t need to seek FDA pre-approval. The FTC doesn’t have a parallel notification requirement for such claims in advertising. Despite this difference, both the FDA and the FTC require that marketers have prior substantiation that the claims are truthful and not misleading. Both agencies apply the same basic principles in assessing the quality and adequacy of the science substantiating those claims. [16]
III. Application of FTC Law to Advertising of Dietary Supplements and Other Health-related Products
To determine whether advertising complies with FTC law, it is first necessary to identify all claims the advertising materials communicate to reasonable consumers. Once the claims are identified, the FTC assesses the scientific evidence upon which the company relies to determine whether there is adequate support for those claims. The following sections describe this two-step process with examples illustrating how the principles of ad interpretation and substantiation apply in the context of advertising for dietary supplements and other health-related products. The examples have been simplified to illustrate one or two specific points. Therefore, advertisers should use these examples as general guidance only.
A. Identifying Claims and Interpreting Ad Meaning
1. Identifying Express and Implied Claims
The first step in evaluating the truthfulness and accuracy of advertising and marketing materials is to identify all express and implied claims conveyed to consumers acting reasonably. Marketers must make sure that whatever they say expressly in advertising is accurate. Often, however, advertising conveys other claims beyond those expressly stated. Under FTC law, a marketer is equally responsible for the accuracy of claims suggested or reasonably implied in advertising. [17] Marketers can’t suggest benefits, safety, or other characteristics about their product indirectly that they couldn’t claim directly.
FTC law focuses not on the marketer’s intent, but on the consumer’s understanding. The determination of what claims are made in marketing is consumer-driven – in other words, what reasonable consumers understand the advertising or marketing materials to communicate about the product. When identifying the claims conveyed by an ad, marketers shouldn’t focus narrowly on individual phrases or statements, but rather should consider each ad as a whole, assessing the “net impression” conveyed by all elements of the ad, including the text, product name, and any charts, graphs, and other images. [18] When an ad lends itself to more than one reasonable interpretation, the advertiser is responsible for substantiating each interpretation.
Furthermore, the FTC views advertising claims from the standpoint of the intended audience. [19] For example, terminally ill consumers might be particularly susceptible to exaggerated cure claims. Extrinsic evidence such as consumer surveys and copy tests can be valuable in determining how consumers interpret certain implied claims. In many cases, however, the claims conveyed are clear enough on the face of an ad, without the need for extrinsic evidence. [20]
Example 1: A brochure for a weight-loss product shows images of doctors in white lab coats looking through microscopes, molecular structures, and a stack of medical journals. These images give an impression of scientific legitimacy and likely convey an implied claim that the product has been clinically proven to be effective for weight loss.
Example 2: A magazine ad for a children’s nutritional drink features an image of the straw from the drink box encircling a child to create a barrier as another child sneezes in her direction. The image used in the ad likely implies that the product can help protect children from catching colds or other airborne infections.
Example 3: An ad for a vitamin supplement claims that 90% of cardiologists regularly take the product. In addition to the express claim about the percentage of cardiologists who use the product, the ad likely conveys an implied claim that the product offers some benefit for the heart.
Example 4: An ad for an infant formula states that an ingredient added to the formula can reduce the symptoms of colic. The ad includes an unrelated chart from a pediatric journal showing that, as a general principle, the length of time that colicky babies cry tends to decrease over the first 12 weeks of life. The graph has nothing to do with the effect of the infant formula on crying; it merely shows that crying decreases as a function of age. Using the graph in an ad for the infant formula likely implies that the formula, rather than the babies’ ages, causes the decrease in crying time.
Depending on how it is phrased or the context in which it is presented, a statement about a product’s effect on the normal “structure or function” of the body may also convey to consumers an implied claim that the product is beneficial for the treatment of a disease. If elements of an ad imply that the product also provides a disease benefit, the advertiser must be able to substantiate the implied disease claim even if the ad contains no express reference to a disease.
Example 5: An ad for an herbal supplement claims that the product boosts the immune system to help maintain a healthy nose and throat during the winter season. The ad features the product name “Cold Away” and includes images of people sneezing and coughing.
